beats.narration: Begin by framing Course Scope and Faculty Flexibility as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Consider this worked case: A faculty member might propose a seminar focused on AI ethics, while another might focus on computer vision, each setting their own prerequisites and assessment methods. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Course Scope and Faculty Flexibility
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create an editable process diagram for Course Scope and Faculty Flexibility with labeled inputs, decisions, state changes, and a checked output.

beats.narration: Now define NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Consider this worked case: Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk, ensuring clear ownership of risk management decisions. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Govern
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a four-step circular diagram labeled Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with arrows indicating the continuous cycle of risk management.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Map operates in a concrete sequence. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Consider this worked case: A team maps a facial recognition system by documenting its intended use in public spaces, the affected population, and potential impacts on privacy and bias. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Map
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist template with fields for context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts, illustrating how to document risk context.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Measure and make the decision criteria explicit. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Consider this worked case: A team measures risk by running quantitative accuracy tests on training data and conducting qualitative interviews with stakeholders to assess fairness and transparency. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Measure
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a split-screen graphic: left side shows quantitative metrics (accuracy, precision, recall), right side shows qualitative indicators (stakeholder feedback, fairness audits, transparency reports).

beats.narration: Apply NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Consider this worked case: A team prioritizes high-risk items, allocates budget for monitoring, and schedules regular audits to track system behavior and context changes. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a risk prioritization matrix with quadrants for likelihood and impact, connected to a resource allocation table and a monitoring schedule.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Machine-Learning Workflow Separation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Consider this worked case: A workflow separates raw data cleaning from model training, ensuring that validation and testing sets remain untouched during hyperparameter tuning. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Machine-Learning Workflow Separation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a linear pipeline diagram with six distinct stages: data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation, with arrows indicating the flow.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Consider this worked case: A supervised method classifies emails as spam or not using labeled data, whereas an unsupervised method clusters customer behavior without predefined categories. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display two side-by-side examples: left shows labeled data points being mapped to classes, right shows unlabeled data points being grouped into clusters.

beats.narration: Use Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Consider this worked case: A team fits a scaling transformer only on the training split, then applies the same transformation to validation and testing data to prevent data leakage. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a diagram of a data pipeline where a preprocessing step is applied only to the training set, with a warning icon indicating that fitting on other data causes leakage.

beats.narration: Connect Pipelines and Cross-Validation to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Consider this worked case: A pipeline ensures that scaling and imputation are applied identically to every fold during cross-validation, preventing inconsistent transformations across splits. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Pipelines and Cross-Validation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a pipeline object with preprocessing steps and an estimator, connected to a cross-validation loop showing multiple data splits being processed through the same pipeline.

beats.narration: Finish with Evaluation Metrics and Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Consider this worked case: A team selects a metric like F1-score for an imbalanced classification task, ensuring that hyperparameter tuning does not influence the final test set evaluation. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Evaluation Metrics and Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist with items: 'Metric matches task', 'Cost of errors considered', 'Hyperparameter selection separate from test evaluation', 'Leakage checked', 'Distribution shift assessed', 'Unexamined assumptions reviewed'.

sources.author: scikit-learn developers
sources.excerpt: Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.
